title: Love for your brother
hookLine: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself
tomorrow: a hard hadith about life and death. what's its heart?

lines: WHAT DO YOU WISH FOR THEM?
cards: Two friends apply for the same internship. One gets it. The other types congrats, with three exclamation points, and means about half of it.
Yesterday's question asked what you wish for the person standing next to you. Anas ibn Malik reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, setting the bar exactly there.
None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.

teach.h: NOT LOVES HIM: LOVES FOR HIM.
teach.b: Not until he loves his brother, which is easy enough on a good day. Loves for him: wants for him the same good he wants for himself. The internship, the health, the good name, the guidance.
And the hadith ties it to faith itself. So who counts as a brother?
In one narration in Sahih Muslim, the wording is: for his neighbor, or he said, for his brother. Some commentators read brother as a fellow believer; others widen it to every person.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an widens the frame on its own, in Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another."
One human family, many tribes, made to meet. Here's ground Muslims share with a neighbor.
The Torah says it in Leviticus, in the JPS 1917 translation: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
And a story in the Talmud has the sage Hillel sum up the Torah for a man in a hurry: what is hateful to you, don't do to your fellow; the rest is commentary, go and learn.
The same bar, in Jewish words: yourself as the measure. And one honest difference.
In Leviticus it comes as a commandment, sealed with I am the LORD. In the hadith it comes as a measure of faith: none of you believes until. One is an order to keep; the other is a mirror to check.

how: Muslims quote this hadith when teaching manners, envy and friendship, as a test for checking one's own heart; some teachers pair it with Qur'an 49:13 on nations and tribes.

games.q: what does “love for your brother” mean?
o: putting other people's needs ahead of your own
wanting for others the good you want for yourself
being kind mainly to the people in your family

games.q: as for yourself — tap the pairs.
p: wants his good, as for himself
what's hateful to you, don't do

s: 'love for your brother' just means being friendly to him
it means wanting for him the good you want for yourself, and the hadith ties it to faith.
one narration in Sahih Muslim says 'his neighbor, or he said, his brother'
and commentators differ on how wide 'brother' reaches.
the Torah's 'love thy neighbour' and this hadith are the same text
two different texts that set the same bar, as yourself: one as a commandment, one as a measure of faith.

games.q: your teammate gets the starting spot you wanted. after the game she's down about a mistake she made. what fits today's hadith?
o: help her get better, the way you'd want someone to help you.
stay polite, but let her figure it out; it's her spot now.
point out the mistake to the coach, since honesty matters most.
games.why: loving for her what you love for yourself means wanting her good, even in the spot you wanted. that's the hadith's measure of faith.

practice: Count three good things you have right now on your fingers: maybe health, a friend, an hour of quiet. For each one, let a face come to mind, someone who could use the same, and wish it for them as fully as you'd want it yourself.
If someone difficult comes to mind, wish it for them too.

wordCard.voice: Love for your brother: wanting for someone else the good you want for yourself. The hadith makes it a measure of faith.

orig.s: لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يُحِبَّ لِأَخِيهِ مَا يُحِبُّ لِنَفْسِهِ
orig.say: laa YU'-mi-nu a-HA-du-kum HAT-taa yu-HIB-ba li-a-KHEE-hi maa yu-HIB-bu li-NAF-sih
orig.note: Arabic: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.

carryVoice: To hold on to: as for myself, the same good I want, wished for the next person too. Fifteen days in.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 13; Sahih Muslim 45 (Anas: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself; in Muslim, 'for his neighbor, or he said, for his brother')

sources.q: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another.
thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; the rest is commentary, go and learn)
